stimulus.source_note: Verbatim excerpts from Henry Cabot Lodge, Senate speech on the League of Nations, August 12, 1919 (public domain). Article X paraphrased from the Covenant of the League of Nations.
stimulus.text:
Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, speech in the Senate on the League of Nations, August 12, 1919 (verbatim excerpts):

"You may call me selfish if you will, conservative or reactionary, or use any other harsh adjective you see fit to apply, but an American I was born and an American I have remained all my life. I can never be anything else but an American, and I must think of the United States first, and when I think of the United States first in an arrangement like this, I am thinking of what is best for the world."

. . .

"I have never had but one allegiance — I cannot divide it now."

The League Covenant's Article X asked member nations to respect and preserve each other's territory against outside attack. Lodge proposed reservations stating that only Congress could commit American forces to such action.

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from Henry Cabot Lodge, Senate speech, August 12, 1919
stem: Lodge's central objection to the League of Nations, as stated in the passage, was that membership would

options.text: force the United States to put the League's demands ahead of American interests
require the United States to pay for all of Europe's war debts
options.misconception: Lodge says nothing about paying Europe's war debts. His objection is about who decides American policy, not about money.

options.text: give Germany a vote over American foreign policy
options.misconception: Germany was not a member of the League when Lodge spoke. His fear was about the League itself, not about Germany voting in it.

options.text: end the Monroe Doctrine by inviting European powers into Latin America
options.misconception: Lodge wanted a reservation protecting the Monroe Doctrine, but the passage itself is about thinking of the United States first. The doctrine is not the objection he states here.

rationales.A: Lodge says he must think of the United States first and cannot divide his allegiance. He feared the League would bind American policy to the decisions of other nations.
rationales.B: Lodge says nothing about paying Europe's war debts. His objection is about who decides American policy, not about money.
rationales.C: Germany was not a member of the League when Lodge spoke. His fear was about the League itself, not about Germany voting in it.
rationales.D: Lodge wanted a reservation protecting the Monroe Doctrine, but the passage itself is about thinking of the United States first. The doctrine is not the objection he states here.
rationales.general:
1. Find what Lodge refuses to divide. His allegiance, which belongs to the United States alone.
2. Find what he puts first. The United States, in any arrangement like the League.
3. Name the fear behind both lines. A league could ask the United States to act against its own interests.
Remember: when a speaker says they cannot divide a loyalty, the fear is that the new commitment will compete with the old one.
